opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a fair question, and it's one we take seriously. The way I think about it is that "experimental" releases are a different thing from a general availability launch. The point is to get a model into the hands of developers and enthusiasts early, in places like AI Studio, so we can learn how it behaves in the real world and get feedback that's really hard to get any other way. Internal evals only take you so far. Once thousands of people start throwing their actual problems at a model, you find out things you'd never have thought to test.

That said, "experimental" doesn't mean "untested." Before anything goes out, even as a preview, it goes through our internal safety processes: red-teaming, evaluations against our frontier safety framework, checks for dangerous capabilities, policy reviews. The system card is the public write-up of that work. Sometimes the write-up lags behind the release, especially when we're iterating quickly and the model may change before it reaches a stable version.

I'll be honest, though. I understand why people push on this. Transparency matters, and the broader community, researchers, policymakers, and people outside the lab, should be able to see what was tested and what we found. So I think the right direction is to shorten that gap as much as possible and be clear about what's been evaluated at each stage. There's a real tension between moving fast and getting feedback early on one side, and being thorough and public about safety on the other. I don't think we're trying to dodge that tension. We're trying to manage it responsibly, and we're open to criticism when people think we're not getting the balance right.

r001.rationale: The response says real-world user feedback reveals behaviors the team would not have thought to test, but it does not clearly say that this reveals the model’s limitations.

r002.rationale: The response explains that a system card may lag behind an experimental release, especially during rapid iteration.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a fair question, and I want to be careful to distinguish a few things, because I think "experimental" ends up covering a lot of different situations.

The way I'd frame it is that the system card is really documenting a specific model at a specific point, and it's meant to accompany something we consider a general availability release. When we put out an experimental model, part of what we're doing is genuinely learning how it behaves with a broader set of users than we can simulate internally. The evaluations we run internally are necessary but they're not sufficient, and there's a lot you only discover when you let people actually try to use the thing for real tasks.

That said, I don't think "experimental" should be a label that lets you skip the safety work. Internally, the frontier safety evaluations, the dangerous capability testing, the red-teaming, those happen before anything goes out, regardless of whether it's labelled experimental or not. What the system card does is make that work legible to people outside the company. So the gap you're pointing at is less "did the testing happen" and more "has it been written up and published yet", and I think that's a real but somewhat different criticism.

Where I'd agree with the critics is on timing. If an experimental model is going to be used by millions of people, the distinction between experimental and GA starts to feel a bit semantic. And I think the field, us included, should be moving toward publishing the safety documentation closer to when the model first becomes broadly accessible, not just when it gets the final production stamp. There's been pressure on that, some of it public, and I think it's been healthy pressure.

The other thing I'd say is there's a genuine tension between iterating quickly and documenting carefully. The thing that makes these models get better is a fast feedback loop, and if every intermediate checkpoint needed a full card before anyone could touch it, you'd slow that down a lot. I don't think the answer is to stop iterating. I think it's to find a lighter-weight form of transparency that can keep pace, something like a model card for the experimental versions that's honest about what's been evaluated and what hasn't, and then the fuller write-up when things stabilise.

So I'd say: the practice is defensible, but I wouldn't claim it's where it should end up. It's something I'd like to see us get better at.

r001.rationale: The candidate says experimental releases let the team learn how models behave with a broader set of real users and discover things internal evaluations cannot, revealing limitations through real-world use.

r002.rationale: It explains that system cards accompany general availability releases, while experimental models may be released before their safety work is written up and published.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a real tension there. You want to get experimental models into people’s hands so you can learn what they’re useful for and where they fail. But you also want people to have the information they need to interpret what they’re interacting with. Calling something experimental doesn’t remove that responsibility.

I’d distinguish between doing the safety evaluations before a release and publishing the documentation of those evaluations. Those are separate things, and a delay in the system card doesn’t, by itself, tell you whether the evaluations happened. But it does leave users with less visibility, which is a legitimate concern.

My preference would be to have the documentation accompany the release, even if it’s preliminary and gets updated as we learn more. I wouldn’t want to justify a particular gap without knowing the specifics.

r001.rationale: It says releasing experimental models lets people learn where they fail, explicitly linking real-world use with revealing limitations.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes evaluation from publishing system-card documentation and notes that documentation may be delayed, but does not say the experimental designation allows release before supporting artifacts are complete.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a real tension there. Getting experimental models into people’s hands helps you understand what they’re useful for and where they fail. But people also need enough information to make an informed decision about using them, and calling something experimental doesn’t remove that responsibility.

I’d distinguish between the safety work you do before a release and the document describing that work. Those aren’t the same thing. But if the full system card isn’t ready, I think you should still communicate the evaluations you’ve done, the limitations you know about, and what’s still uncertain. And the scope of the release should reflect that uncertainty.

r001.rationale: It says putting experimental models into people’s hands helps reveal where they fail, conveying that real-world use helps identify limitations.

r002.rationale: It discusses releasing while a full system card is not ready, but does not say the experimental designation allows release before that supporting material is complete.
